extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, patent owners/patentees, and USPTO examiners/Board members involved in interference proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards governing how patent interferences are suggested, declared, and litigated before the Board (new part 41 rules), including threshold issues, priority showings, claim/count correspondence, and motions practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description as a threshold issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description may be treated as a threshold issue under § 41.201, narrowed to provoked interferences where applicants copy claims to provoke an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description addresses the problem complementary to repose under 35 U.S.C. 135(b): the claim was timely, but lacks an adequate written description. The provision is narrowed to provoked interferences because of concern applicants would copy claims merely to provoke inter partes administrative challenges. The Office will not examine an applicant’s intent to provoke an interference where the opportunity to have done so is clear; otherwise practice would be open to abuse and misconduct. (Cites Snitzer v. Etzel and policy discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement as a possible threshold issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement can be included among the list of threshold issues since the list is inclusive, but routine treatment of enablement as a threshold issue is left to adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current impression is enablement appears to be less frequently abused in provoking interferences (in the absence of lack of written description). Whether enablement becomes a routine threshold issue will develop through cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must propose at least one count when suggesting an interference (§41.202(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant suggesting an interference must propose at least one count because an explanation of correspondence to the count is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 41.202(a)(2) modified to clarify this requirement, since §41.202(a)(3) requires correspondence explanation. The requirement ensures suggested counts are presented so correspondence can be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify interfering claims and explain correspondence (§41.202(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant suggesting an interference must identify the claims that interfere and explain how they correspond to the suggested count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the suggestion is made based on a published application, the decision to declare an interference is based on claims pending in the published application at the time of the decision (which may differ from the published claims). No interference will be declared until both applications have allowable claims that still interfere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why applicant will prevail on priority (§41.202(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant suggesting an interference must provide a detailed explanation of why it will prevail on priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 41.202(a)(4) is a general requirement; if the applicant has the earliest effective filing date the explanation should be simple. This is distinct from §41.202(d), which requires an actual showing of priority when the applicant does not have the earlier effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chart/supporting disclosure showing: constructive reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When showing supporting disclosure for an embodiment within the scope of interfering subject matter, the rule refers to a constructive reduction to practice within the scope of the interfering subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition of constructive reduction to practice in §41.201 was clarified to reflect anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1); this change addresses concerns about narrowness when only entire subject matter (not a specific embodiment) is disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentees seeking interferences: alternative remedies (§41.202(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The process for suggesting an interference is not available to a patentee; patentees are pointed to alternative remedies (§1.99 and §1.291).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 41.202(b) revised to clarify intent and to point patentees to both §1.99 and §1.291. The rule is not intended to modify remedies available under those provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner requirement to add an interfering claim (§41.202(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may require an applicant to add an interfering claim; the applicant must either comply by adding the proposed claim (or a better claim) or contest the requirement, with possible consequences for refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant’s remedy is to comply or to add a better claim or contest. Refusal to copy a supported claim can result in disclaimer (In re Ogiue). §41.202(c) modified to require showings like §41.202(a)(2)–(a)(6) when the interference would be with a patent. Disputes as to satisfaction of procedural requirements may be petitioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority showing requirement when applicant lacks earlier effective filing date (§41.202(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant does not have the earlier effective filing date, a more thorough showing of priority is required under §41.202(d) because on the face of the record no interference is necessary otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no inconsistency with §41.202(a)(4): the former is general, the latter addresses the case lacking an earlier effective filing date. The three-month reduced showing practice under §1.608 was eliminated—it was considered meaningless across technologies and could equally apply to the earlier-filing party, failing to resolve first-to-invent issues. Distinguishing simple vs complex technologies is unworkable; waiting until after declaration is problematic because inadequate early showings trigger summary disposition and would prolong interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence sufficient to show priority; proffer when subpoena required (§41.202(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 41.202(e) addresses what evidence suffices to show priority; when necessary evidence is unavailable without a subpoena, a detailed proffer of expected testimony or production may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (2) added for situations where showing cannot be made because evidence is not available without subpoena; in such cases, a detailed proffer may be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering subject matter defined by two-way test (§41.203(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board uses a two-way test for interfering subject matter rather than a one-way test, because a one-way test would turn many 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections into interferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-way test is not workable; two-way test long implicit in no interference-in-fact standards. The two-way test is narrower and prevents over-declaration of interferences. Case law cited (e.g., Winter v. Fujita, Aelony v. Arni) and statutory comparison to 35 U.S.C. 291.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of directional (one-way) no-interference-in-fact test
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed directional test (movant shows its claim is patentably distinct, not both directions) is rejected because it cedes control to the species claimant and ignores the Director’s role under 35 U.S.C. 135(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under a directional test an interference could simultaneously exist and not exist; such a result would be unfair and enlist the Director on one party’s side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish claim dominance from interference
rubrics_metrics.description: A senior party seeking to attack a junior patentee with a dominating claim should pursue claim dominance remedies (e.g., reexamination or post-grant review), not an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference is not a post-grant cancellation proceeding; Office proposed post-grant review to address such concerns. The Office remains steadfast on this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority proofs are governed by statute (102(g)(1) vs 102(g)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in treatment of foreign priority proofs under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1) and (g)(2) reflect statutory choices and, if problematic, should be addressed by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even assuming perceived unfairness, the legislative decision created the distinction; Office cannot eliminate a statutory difference by rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unpatentable claims in declaring interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, claims that are unpatentable would not be placed into an interference; if all interfering claims become unpatentable via a threshold motion, judgment in the interference is justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See §41.102 and cited cases (Brenner v. Manson; Berman v. Housey). The Board will not generally include unpatentable claims in an interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of declaration need not explain basis for correspondence/benefit (§41.203(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of declaration need not set forth the basis for any claim correspondence or accorded benefit; prior attempts caused delays without much benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaration creates presumptions that are developed through motions; parties will have an opportunity to address presumptions before any rejection or cancellation of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding patents or applications to an interference (§41.203(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to add a patent or application may be raised any time but is more likely to be granted if raised early; substitutions can be achieved by adding a second application and cancelling the first contingent on the addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule addresses addition of patents/applications (not substitution directly). The intent is to mirror the decision process for declaring an interference; timing and early filing weigh in favor of granting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of non-party patents/applications: movant need not show patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule permits adding non-party patents/applications to an interference; the movant is not required to show the added patent’s or application’s claims are patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings where a third party is not a participant are not appropriate forums to explore patentability of that third party’s claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority statement requirements (§41.204(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party that will put on a priority case must file a priority statement listing specific requirements and stating bases for relief (e.g., intent to prove derivation or to seek benefit of additional constructive reduction to practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 41.204(a) amended to list specific requirements for the priority statement. It still requires the party to state the bases on which it believes it is entitled to relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties bound by preliminary statements; senior parties' obligations (§41.120(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are bound by their preliminary statements; senior parties do not need to file a priority statement if they do not intend to put on a priority case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section clarifies binding effect of preliminary statements and when priority statements are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions list content and timing (§41.204(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The motions list required under §41.204(b) must provide sufficient detail (more than current practice) to place the Board and the opponent on notice of the precise relief sought and facilitate scheduling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is not a substitute for a motion but must enable the Board to schedule and the opponent to prepare; detailed lists can produce efficiencies such as stipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of order of invention when constructive reduction dates identical (§41.207(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: When both parties have identical dates for constructive reduction to practice and neither elects to put on a priority case, neither is entitled to a presumption of priority (codifies case law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule codifies case law (Van Otteren v. Hafner; Lassman v. Brossi) where both parties with same date of reduction to practice were not entitled to presumptions and both lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened evidentiary standard for late filers (§41.207(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a junior applicant first files after the senior party’s patent issues (or after publication of a senior application), the priority case of the late filer is subject to the clear and convincing evidence standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: consistent with Price v. Symsek and older precedent—concerns about presumption of validity, spurring, and degradation of evidence after delay. Publication treated similarly to patent issuance for triggering heightened scrutiny; rule does not create a patentability bar but triggers higher scrutiny to encourage prompt filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim correspondence estoppel and generic/species concerns (§41.207(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that loses a count may be estopped from later claiming subject matter patentably indistinct from the lost count; generic claims corresponding to a species count face a presumption that must be rebutted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §41.207(b) formalizes estoppel effects (citing In re Deckler and Saunders). If concerned, a party may move to have a generic claim designated as not corresponding to a species count; often deferred until the priority phase and relief may be granted with proof that the generic invention antedates the lost species count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of presumption of abandonment/suppression for long delays (§41.207(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed presumption of abandonment, suppression, or concealment for filings more than one year after actual reduction to practice was deleted as unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays longer than 18 months often result in a statutory bar or heightened scrutiny anyway. Under motions practice, abandonment/suppression/ concealment may be raised in opposition to a priority motion; any discovery or compelled testimony motions should be filed promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of §41.208(a)(2): definition of interfering subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: §41.208(a)(2) was reworded to emphasize the 'definition of the interfering subject matter' rather than 'count' to focus parties on using substantive motions to define admissible proofs for priority before the priority phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The point is to define the range of admissible proofs for priority early, simplifying the priority contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority as a motion under preliminary motions practice (§41.208(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority may be contested in the form of motions and need not be decided simultaneously with preliminary motions; the Board may handle priority with, or instead of, preliminary motions on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions practice is more efficient: each movant must explain the evidence it relies on rather than dumping it on opponents. Typical flow: junior party files motion with evidence, senior party files its election/motion if it presents a case, oppositions and replies follow. Motions process can eliminate later briefing after evidence service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability showing when adding or amending claims/counts (§41.208(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a claim or count is added or amended, the movant must show that the claim or count does not run afoul of any known patentability problem; §41.208(c) is limited to this patentability showing requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement often obliges proving a negative; acceptable alternatives include showing unawareness of a basis for unpatentability. Where prior prosecution or an opponent’s motion raised a patentability question, the movant must address that specific issue. For claims, movant must show where written description can be found (§41.110(c)(2)). For counts, a broadened count must be patentable over prior art so embodiments unpatentable over prior art cannot be used to prove priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor in interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a high duty of candor toward the Board in contested cases; a separate codified rule like §1.56/§1.555 is unnecessary because litigants and counsel already owe a duty of candor and the Board can sanction misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board authority to sanction misconduct (§41.128(a)) and to regulate counsel (§41.5) will be used to address candor violations. Limited discovery in Board proceedings increases the duty of candor. The Office has proposed broader disciplinary rules but did not adopt a narrow codification here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and procedural scope of new part 41
rubrics_metrics.description: Major rule changes consolidate ex parte appeals, inter partes reexamination appeals, and patent interference rules into a new part 41, with Subparts for general Board provisions, ex parte appeals, inter partes reexamination appeals, contested cases, and interference-specific practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable changes: delegation to Chief Administrative Patent Judge for certain petitions, limited amendments filed after filing a brief, changed format/content of appeal brief, clarified when interference-in-fact exists, clarified claim correspondence and benefit of earlier applications, requirements when adding a claim to provoke an interference, and use of a two-way unpatentability test. These are interpretative/rules of practice and procedure under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A).
